question.text: This Mesopotamian civilization contained the city of Ashur and had rulers like Tigaleth-Pileser and Sennacherib. Its capital, Nineveh (NIN-ih-veh), hosted the largest library in the world at the time, built by Ashurbanipal.
question.clue: Accounts of invasions by this empire written by king Taharqa record that its armies had their bowstrings eaten by field mice.

swap.leadin: Name these people who all formulated their own law codes.
swap.text: This Babylonian king created a namesake law code that demanded "an eye for an eye."
swap.clue: This Amorite king went up a mountain to receive a stele from the sun god Shamash that was later discovered in Susa.

question.text: This Mesopotamiam civilization is the earliest known human civilization. This civilization, whose city-states included Ur, developed the cuneiform writing system.
question.clue: A tomb built by this culture contains several ornate lyres, as well as dozens of handmaidens who were sacrificed and buried in a "Death Pit."

swap.leadin: This city re-entered prominence as the capital of the Chaldean empire.
swap.text: Name this city. The Weidner Chronicle suggests that Sargon built this city, and according to legend Queen Amytis missed her home so much that her husband Nebuchadnezzar II built hanging gardens here.
swap.clue: This city's Processional Way was added to during its Chaldean dynasty by a structure on which rows of brick reliefs of animals decorated a massive blue tiled gate.

question.leadin: In the Bible, this powerful leader brought the Hebrews into Babylon as slaves.
question.text: Name this Neo-Babylonian ruler who constructed the Hanging Gardens as a gift for his wife.
question.clue: This son of Nabopolassar was stricken with insanity for seven years of his reign.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about Mesopotamia's earliest civilization, Sumer.
swap.text: This Akkadian conqueror of Sumer is said to have founded the world's first empire. This king's daughter Enheduanna is the first recorded poet in history.
swap.answerHtml: Sargon of Akkad [accept Sargon the Great or Sargon I]
swap.clue: This ruler famously defeated Lugal-Zage-Si of Umma, the last Sumerian King.

question.leadin: This term, which designates much of the Levant, was coined in the early 1900s by archaeologist James Henry Breasted.
question.text: Give this two-word English name for the "cradle of civilization" that spanned the lower Nile and Mesopotamia.
question.clue: This region in the Middle East that gets its name from its shape and rich soil, sometimes known as the "cradle of civilization".

swap.text: Ur was home to one of these structures. These structures were large stepped pyramids built by the Sumerian peoples for worship.
swap.clue: Koldewey also found one that he took to be a temple to Marduk, the name of which, Etemenanki, translates as "The Foundation of Heaven and Earth."

question.leadin: A magnificent blue and gold copy of this structure can be found opposite the Market gate of Miletus in the Pergamon Museum.
question.text: Name this gate that was once built into the wall that surrounded Babylon. It is named for a deity.
question.clue: This large blue and gold structure located in Babylon. The walls lining the street leading up to this structure were decorated with a brick mosaic of lions and flowers.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the profession of the scribe.
swap.text: Assyrian or Babylonian scribes probably also produced works in the namesake language of this empire which was commonly spoken throughout Mesopotamia. The founder of this empire, Sargon the Great, won the Battle of Uruk.
swap.clue: Its most famous ruler's life was detailed on the Ebla tablets, and started out as a cup-bearer to Ur-Zababa of Kish.

question.text: The older Babylonian empire placed great importance on the control of the priesthood in the city of Nippur. This Akkadian king and grandfather of Naram-Sin is thought to have begun the practice of installing his daughter in the position.
question.clue: He appointed his daughter Enheduanna high priestess, and his empire reached its greatest expanse under his grandson Naram-sin.

swap.text: Dally claims the Hanging Gardens were really built in this city, as evidenced by retranslated inscriptions and a bas-relief showing a terraced garden. Sennacherib brought this capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire to regional prominence.
swap.clue: This city was sacked by a coalition including Scythians assembled in 612 BC by the Median king Cyaxares ("kye-ax-AIR-ees"), ending the dominance of a line that included Tiglath-Pileser III.

question.leadin: In 1852, Hormuzd Rassam discovered a second section of this institution in the Ottoman Vilayet of Mosul.
question.text: Name this collection whose discovery is attributed to Assyriologist Austen Layard. This collection found at the site of Nineveh included copies of the Enuma Elish and Poor Man of Nippur.
question.clue: Like a similar institution at Tell el-Amarna, this institution preserved one of the only known versions of "Adapa and the South Wind" as well as several objects "baked" in a post-Carcemish sack.

swap.leadin: In one tomb, this archaeologist discovered a headdress made of golden leaves, four stringed lyres, and a golden and lapis lazuli encrusted bull's head.
swap.text: Name this British archaeologist who in 1922 led an excavation of the Sumerian city of Ur.
swap.clue: This archaeologist made a name for himself by discovering the Great Ziggurat and other buildings at Ur, a Sumerian city then thought to be the world's oldest.

question.text: The title "King of the Universe" has been compared to the similar title of "King of" these figurative places, indicating rule over the known world. These places included Subartu ("soob-AR-too") in the north and Elam ("ih-LAHM") in the east, and Hammurabi claimed to have "made [these places] obedient".
question.answerHtml: the four corners of the world [accept four regions or four quarters; accept titles such as King of the Four Corners of the World/Universe; accept lugal-an-ub-da-limmu-ba or šarru kibrat 'arbaim or šar kibrāti arba'i or šar kibrāt erbetti; prompt on corners or regions or quarters (of the world) alone]
question.answer: the four corners of the world

swap.text: The Commagene capital of Samosata was located on the banks of this river. This river and the Tigris River provided sustenance to Mesopotamian civilizations.
swap.clue: Yazid I of the Umayyads defeated a small army belonging to Muhammad's grandson at Karbala, which is near this river. This river roughly parallels the Tigris River.

question.leadin: The Amarna letters contain a diplomatic correspondence between Amenhotep III and a king of this Hurrian polity named Tushratta.
question.text: Identify this Mesopotamian kingdom with capital at Washukanni. Its greatest king was Saustatar.
question.clue: King Tushratta of this kingdom attempted to solidify an alliance with Egypt through the marriage of his daughter but he was assassinated by one of his sons after the fall of Carchemish.

swap.leadin: Dominant rulers gradually claimed this title instead of ensi, which kings of Isin and Larsa took as pious stewards of a temple's farmlands.
swap.text: Give this Sumerian title that precedes "Anne-Mundu" to identify a "king of the four corners" from Adab, "Zage-Si" to identify a warlord overthrown by Sargon, and "banda" to identify a mythical king of Uruk.

question.leadin: This kingdom's capital was Washukanni. FTPE.
question.text: Name this Ancient Near Eastern Empire, noted for its rivalry with the Hittites, Assyrians, and Egyptians.
question.clue: Thutmose IV proposed seven times to marry a princess of this polity, and some scholars have identified Nefertiti with a princess of this polity named Tadukhipa.

swap.text: A king of Lagash with this prefix in his name looms over his subjects in a kaunakes skirt in the "perforated relief." This prefix appears in the name of the founder of the Third Dynasty, who created the world's oldest law code.
swap.clue: A king named -Nammu, who founded a dynasty that supplanted Lagash and the Gutians, was succeeded by Shulgi.
